title: AF-1-part-1
description: Airframe exam covering fuselage, wing, empennage, landing gear, control surfaces, doors/windows, structural design philosophy, and related airframe systems, drawn from the AF-1 question/answer bank.

questions.question: Antidrag wires resist the forward and aft forces in the wing structure in which direction?
questions.explanation: Antidrag wires run chordwise between the front and rear spars to resist drag loads acting along the chord direction.

questions.question: A triple-pane acrylic cabin window primarily provides what benefit?
questions.explanation: The extra acrylic pane in a triple-pane window arrangement adds sound/thermal insulation, including attenuating engine noise.

questions.question: Requirements for tabs, door operation, and control surfaces are published under which regulation?
options: A. FAA Part 25, for aircraft above 5,700 kg
B. FAA Part 23, for aircraft below 5,700 kg
C. FAA Part 43, for all aircraft
questions.explanation: FAR Part 25 covers airworthiness standards for transport category airplanes, generally those above 5,700 kg (12,500 lb).

questions.question: Fuselage skin thickness varies along a particular location mainly based on what?
options: B. The load carried and stress sustained at that location
C. The cabin temperature at that location
questions.explanation: Skin gauge is selected according to the structural load and stress the section must carry, so thickness varies by location.

questions.question: Aircraft windshields must comply with regulations addressing which hazard?
questions.explanation: Windshields must meet bird-strike resistance requirements to protect the flight deck during impact at operating speeds.

questions.question: On the standard aircraft zonal numbering system, Zone 400 generally represents which area?
questions.explanation: In the ATA/manufacturer zonal numbering convention, the 400-series zone numbers are typically assigned to the power plant/engine area.

questions.question: Wings that have no external bracing (struts or wires) are called what?
questions.explanation: A full cantilever wing carries all bending and torsional loads internally without external struts or wires.

questions.question: The wing has its cambered aerodynamic shape mainly because of which structural member?
questions.explanation: Wing ribs are shaped to the airfoil section and maintain the cambered profile of the wing skin.

questions.question: A ruddervator (combined rudder and elevator surface) is found on which type of empennage?
questions.explanation: A V-tail arrangement combines the functions of rudder and elevator into two surfaces called ruddervators.

questions.question: A compression rib or bulkhead rib is designed to receive compression loads that tend to do what?
options: A. Force the wing spars apart
B. Force the wing spars together
questions.explanation: Compression ribs resist loads that would otherwise push the front and rear spars toward each other.

questions.question: What is the first step when installing a stabilizer?
questions.explanation: Before installation, the mounting points and structure must be inspected to ensure they are airworthy and ready to accept the stabilizer.

questions.question: How many structural members make up the primary structure of a typical transport fuselage?
options: B. Five (frames, stringers, skin, floor, and doors)
C. Three (fuselage frames, main floor members, main spars)
questions.explanation: The primary load path is commonly described as fuselage frames, main floor beams, and main spars/structure.

questions.question: What is a key difference between rotary-wing and fixed-wing aircraft?
options: B. Fixed-wing aircraft do not need an airfoil
C. Fixed-wing aircraft need forward motion to generate lift
questions.explanation: A fixed wing generates lift only when air flows over it due to forward motion, while a rotor can generate lift while the aircraft is stationary.

questions.question: The wing is especially vulnerable to accidental damage during which ground operations?
questions.explanation: Wingtips and leading edges are commonly struck during taxiing and towing due to their span and proximity to other objects.

questions.question: Occupants of an aircraft are protected from electrical shock (e.g., lightning) because the surrounding structure acts as what?
questions.explanation: The metal aircraft structure encloses the occupants like a Faraday cage, conducting lightning current around rather than through the cabin.

questions.question: Precipitation static charge on an aircraft is produced by what mechanism?
options: A. The batteries overcharging in flight
B. The aircraft moving through the air absorbs electrons from the atmosphere (friction with precipitation/particles)
C. The engines generating excess current
questions.explanation: Friction between the airframe and airborne particles (rain, snow, dust) causes a transfer of electrons, building up a static charge.

questions.question: Vertical loads in the fuselage are primarily concentrated on which members?
questions.explanation: Frames and formers are oriented to pick up vertical (and circumferential) loads and transfer them into the fuselage shell.

questions.question: In which type of fuselage construction are longerons used as the primary load-carrying members?
questions.explanation: In a truss-type fuselage, longerons (and their associated truss members) carry the primary loads, with the covering carrying little load.

questions.question: Which type of flap both increases wing area and changes wing camber when extended?
questions.explanation: A Fowler flap slides aft and down, increasing both wing area and camber, unlike a plain or split flap which only changes camber.

questions.question: Ribs found at the inboard edge of the wing, where the wing attaches to the fuselage, are called what?
questions.explanation: Butt ribs are located at the wing root/inboard edge where the wing structure attaches to the fuselage.

questions.question: Nosing over and ground looping are problems most associated with which landing gear configuration?
questions.explanation: Conventional gear places the center of gravity behind the main wheels, making the aircraft prone to nosing over and ground looping.

questions.question: Lateral (roll) stability of an aircraft is significantly affected by which design feature?
questions.explanation: Dihedral angle creates a restoring roll moment when the aircraft sideslips, improving lateral stability.

questions.question: Which landing gear configuration allows forceful brake application without the risk of the aircraft nosing over?
questions.explanation: With tricycle gear the CG is forward of the main gear, allowing heavy braking without tipping the aircraft onto its nose.

questions.question: Which device assists the pilot in moving a control surface at very high airspeeds?
questions.explanation: A spring tab uses a spring linkage to provide additional aerodynamic assistance to the pilot's control input, especially important at high speed.

questions.question: Which wing planform is characterized by a low aspect ratio?
questions.explanation: A delta wing has a short span relative to its chord, giving it a low aspect ratio compared with straight or elliptical wings.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement about ventilating internal structural cavities?
options: A. That ventilation is meant to prevent corrosion
B. That ventilation helps remove moisture from enclosed spaces
C. That ventilation can help balance pressure within the structure
questions.explanation: Trapped moisture, not the absence of ventilation itself, is the real corrosion driver; the statement singling out "prevent corrosion" as the sole/defining purpose is the incorrect one among the listed options.

questions.question: Aircraft that carry passengers and crew must have seats that comply with what kind of regulations?
questions.explanation: Passenger and crew seats must meet crashworthiness standards covering strength, attachment, and occupant protection during an emergency landing.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT typically found on a full (pure) monocoque fuselage?
questions.explanation: A pure monocoque relies on the skin and formers/frames to carry loads; it does not use longerons as primary load-carrying members.

questions.question: Which parts of the aircraft are classified as secondary structure?
options: A. Parts that carry no load at all
B. Parts that are highly stressed but, if damaged, will not cause failure of the aircraft
C. Parts that are never inspected
questions.explanation: Secondary structure can be highly loaded locally, but its failure does not lead to loss of the aircraft, unlike primary structure.

questions.question: Redundant structural or system designs are characteristic of which design philosophy?
questions.explanation: Fail-safe design provides multiple load paths or redundancy so that failure of one element does not cause overall failure.

questions.question: Precise points on an aircraft are located using a system of what reference lines?
options: A. Fuselage stations, water lines, and buttock lines
questions.explanation: Aircraft dimensional references use fuselage (body) stations, water lines, and buttock lines to precisely locate structure and equipment.

questions.question: In which type of fuselage construction does the skin act as the primary load carrier?
questions.explanation: In pure monocoque construction, the stressed skin alone carries the primary bending, shear, and torsional loads.

questions.question: A firewall is typically constructed from which materials?
questions.explanation: Firewalls must resist fire penetration, so they are made from fire-resistant materials such as stainless steel or titanium.

questions.question: What promotes the smooth flow of air over gaps between fixed and movable control surfaces?
questions.explanation: Gap seals close the space between a fixed surface and its adjacent movable control surface, smoothing airflow and reducing drag/noise.

questions.question: Engine mounts and fuselage frames are classified as what kind of structure?
questions.explanation: Primary structure carries flight, ground, and pressurization loads whose failure would endanger the aircraft; engine mounts and fuselage frames fall into this category.

questions.question: In a Warren truss arrangement, the diagonal wires/members primarily carry what type of stress?
questions.explanation: In the classic Warren truss pattern, the diagonal members are generally designed to carry tension loads as the structure flexes.

questions.question: In a pressurized aircraft, drain tubes are typically fitted with what feature?
questions.explanation: Drain tubes in a pressurized fuselage include a drain/check valve so cabin pressure is not lost while moisture is still able to drain overboard.

questions.question: Which high-lift device is controlled independently by its own dedicated switch in the cockpit?
questions.explanation: On many transport aircraft, leading-edge slats have a separate control switch/system distinct from the trailing-edge flap system.

questions.question: A key design feature of acrylic cabin windows is what?
questions.explanation: Acrylic windows are designed fail-safe, typically using multiple panes so that failure of one pane does not result in loss of cabin pressure.

questions.question: Aircraft doors are constructed with inner and outer skins and vertical/horizontal members similar to which other structure?
questions.explanation: Doors are essentially small fuselage sections, built with inner/outer skins and a supporting frame similar to the surrounding fuselage structure.

questions.question: A small hydraulic shock absorber mounted between the nose wheel fork and the nose gear cylinder/structure is called what?
questions.explanation: A shimmy damper controls rapid, unwanted oscillation (shimmy) of the nose wheel by damping its side-to-side motion.

questions.question: Bonding cables on an aircraft are more correctly referred to as what?
questions.explanation: Bonding jumpers/cables are secondary current-carrying paths used to maintain electrical continuity between structural components.

questions.question: An aircraft windshield must be able to withstand impacts at approximately what speed range?
questions.explanation: Transport category windshields are certified to withstand bird strikes and other impacts in roughly the 250-350 knot range typical of low-altitude operations.

questions.question: What makes it easy to load freight onto the cargo floor of an aircraft?
options: A. A smooth painted floor only
questions.explanation: Cargo floors incorporate roller trays, guides, and powered or manual systems to let freight be moved and loaded with ground equipment such as trucks.

questions.question: The cambered shape of a wing cross-section is called what?
questions.explanation: The cambered cross-sectional shape of a wing or control surface is called an airfoil.

questions.question: Which type of tab does NOT have a dedicated control from the cockpit?
questions.explanation: Balance tabs move automatically with the primary control surface to reduce control forces; they are not independently operated from the cockpit like trim tabs.

questions.question: The width of the wing measured parallel to the longitudinal axis (leading edge to trailing edge) is called what?
questions.explanation: Chord is the straight-line distance from the leading edge to the trailing edge of an airfoil section.

questions.question: A device that creates a swirling, downward vortex to help maintain attached boundary layer flow over the wing is called what?
questions.explanation: Vortex generators create small, energetic vortices that re-energize the boundary layer, helping delay flow separation over the wing.

questions.question: Which device reduces drag caused by wingtip vortices in flight?
questions.explanation: Winglets reduce the strength of wingtip vortices and the resulting induced drag by altering the spanwise airflow at the tip.

questions.question: What type of stress acts on the upper surface of the wing skin during flight (wing bending upward)?
questions.explanation: As the wing bends upward under lift, the upper skin is placed in compression while the lower skin is placed in tension.

questions.question: A 4130 (chrome-moly) steel tubing structural member is typically designed to carry which types of load?
questions.explanation: Welded steel tube members in truss structures are generally designed to carry axial tension and compression loads.

questions.question: Approximately how much current can a lightning strike deliver to an aircraft structure?
questions.explanation: A typical severe lightning strike can involve peak currents on the order of 100,000 amperes, which the airframe must safely conduct away.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a ball-mat in the cargo compartment?
options: A. To let freight be easily rotated/maneuvered
B. To weigh the cargo automatically
C. To seal the cargo door
questions.explanation: A ball-mat (ball transfer mat) uses recessed balls to let heavy cargo containers or pallets be turned and positioned with minimal effort.

questions.question: Which aircraft structural element does NOT support ground or flight loads?
questions.explanation: Fairings are aerodynamic covers that smooth airflow but are not designed to carry structural flight or ground loads.

questions.question: A structure or component given a certified period of operation during which failure is considered extremely unlikely, accounting for wear, fatigue, and corrosion, follows which design concept?
questions.explanation: Safe-life parts are retired after a defined service life calculated so that the probability of fatigue failure within that life is extremely low.

questions.question: Which door is used by both crew and passengers for normal boarding?
questions.explanation: The passenger entry door is the main boarding door used by crew and passengers during normal ground operations.

questions.question: While designing the passenger compartment, seats must be able to withstand a sudden stop of over how many times the force of gravity?
questions.explanation: Modern crashworthy seat standards require seats and attachments to withstand dynamic loads of roughly 16g (commonly cited around 20g in training material) in a sudden-stop scenario.

questions.question: In the entrance door area, what is installed to allow freight to be loaded easily?
questions.explanation: A ball-mat near the entrance/cargo door lets containers and pallets be rolled and rotated into position with minimal force.

questions.question: What is the first step in the installation of a wing?
questions.explanation: The wing must first be properly supported (e.g., on a stand or hoist) before attachment points are aligned and fastened.

questions.question: An airworthiness certificate must conform to what?
options: A. The airline's internal maintenance schedule
C. The type of certificate (type certificate) issued for that aircraft
questions.explanation: The airworthiness certificate is issued based on the aircraft's conformity with its type certificate and approved design data.

questions.question: What structural members give the fuselage its shape?
questions.explanation: Formers and frames establish the cross-sectional shape of the fuselage, over which the skin is applied.

questions.question: What is the first step when removing a control surface?
questions.explanation: Before any disassembly work, applicable safety procedures (locking controls, tagging, support) must be observed first.

questions.question: What is the use of the buttock line reference system?
options: A. To measure altitude above the ground
B. To measure engine thrust line only
C. To locate structures to the right or left of the aircraft, with the fuselage centerline as station zero
questions.explanation: Buttock lines are measured left and right from the fuselage centerline (buttock line zero) to precisely locate structure laterally.

questions.question: Passenger seat mechanisms can be disconnected from the floor, if necessary, by doing what?
options: A. Releasing a few quick-release fasteners
C. Removing the cabin floor panel
questions.explanation: Seat tracks and attachment fittings are designed with quick-release fasteners so seats can be removed or repositioned quickly.

questions.question: How is the angle of incidence of a wing measured?
options: A. Between the wingtip and the wing root
B. Between the horizontal stabilizer and the wing
C. Between the wing chord line and the fuselage longitudinal axis
questions.explanation: Angle of incidence is the fixed angle between the wing's chord line and the fuselage reference (longitudinal) axis.

questions.question: Which type of wing requires additional external support?
questions.explanation: A semi-cantilever wing uses external struts or wires in addition to its internal structure, unlike a full cantilever wing.

questions.question: A distance measured from a reference line along the longitudinal axis of the fuselage is called what?
questions.explanation: Fuselage/body stations measure distance fore and aft along the longitudinal axis from a defined reference datum.

questions.question: In a wire-braced structure, the bracing wire is designed to carry what type of load?
questions.explanation: Bracing wires can only pull, so they are designed to carry tension loads, typically arranged so at least one wire is always in tension.

questions.question: Which of the following fuselage requirements is NOT mandatory for all aircraft?
options: A. That it must be pressurized
B. That it must support flight loads
C. That it must protect the occupants
questions.explanation: Pressurization is required only for aircraft operating at altitudes where cabin pressurization is needed; it is not a universal fuselage requirement.

questions.question: What device is used to control the spanwise flow of air over a swept wing?
questions.explanation: A wing fence is a stationary vane on the wing's upper surface that blocks spanwise airflow, helping prevent tip stall on swept wings.

questions.question: The Pratt truss type of construction is known for having what members?
options: C. Longerons, diagonal members, and vertical members
questions.explanation: A Pratt truss uses longerons connected by vertical and diagonal members arranged to carry tension and compression efficiently.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a combined stress condition?
options: A. Pure tension in a bolt
B. Pure compression in a strut
questions.explanation: Wing bending combines tension on one surface with compression on the opposite surface plus shear, making it a combined-stress condition.

questions.question: Which of the following aircraft is designed to be supported in the air by the buoyancy principle?
questions.explanation: A balloon is lighter-than-air and is supported by buoyancy, unlike heavier-than-air aircraft that rely on aerodynamic lift.

questions.question: Width measurements taken to the left and right of the fuselage centerline are referred to as what?
questions.explanation: Buttock line dimensions describe lateral distance left or right of the fuselage centerline (buttock line zero).

questions.question: A control surface that can be adjusted independently from the cockpit to relieve control pressures is called what?
questions.explanation: A trim tab is pilot-adjustable from the cockpit and is used to relieve control-wheel/pedal forces in steady flight.

questions.question: Which of the following is a required criterion for the cockpit compartment?
options: A. It must be an enclosed compartment
B. It must be located aft of the wing
C. It must be pressurized on all aircraft types
questions.explanation: Flight deck design requirements call for the cockpit to be an enclosed compartment, among other crew-protection criteria.

questions.question: To prevent leakage of cabin pressure, all doors must have what feature?
questions.explanation: Pressurized aircraft doors require an effective, substantial seal around the frame to prevent cabin pressure loss.

questions.question: Which of the following aircraft is designed to be supported in the air by dynamic reaction with the air?
questions.explanation: A glider (and heavier-than-air aircraft generally) is supported by the dynamic reaction of air flowing over its wings, unlike buoyant craft like balloons.

questions.question: Which structural component does NOT carry flight loads?
questions.explanation: The landing gear primarily carries ground loads (taxi, takeoff/landing impact) rather than in-flight aerodynamic loads.

questions.question: What methodology helps determine the load to be imposed on every part of the aircraft structure?
questions.explanation: Stress analysis is the engineering methodology used to determine the loads and resulting stresses that each structural member must withstand.

questions.question: Which of the following comes first when removing a stabilizer?
questions.explanation: Before unbolting the stabilizer, its control cables (elevator/trim linkages) must be disconnected to avoid damage or injury.

questions.question: What is the principal structural member of the wing?
questions.explanation: The spar is the main structural member running spanwise that carries the primary bending and shear loads of the wing.

questions.question: Fuselage construction in which the skin carries all the loads without supporting structure is called what?
questions.explanation: In pure monocoque construction, there is no internal truss or stringer framework; the stressed skin alone carries all loads.

questions.question: Which tab moves in the same direction as the primary control surface it is attached to?
questions.explanation: An anti-servo tab deflects in the same direction as the control surface to increase the force the pilot must apply, improving feel/stability.

questions.question: How do spoilers assist the roll movement of the aircraft?
options: A. On the wing where the aileron moves up, the spoiler also rises, further reducing lift on that wing
B. They deploy symmetrically on both wings during roll
C. They only operate during landing roll-out
questions.explanation: Roll spoilers deploy on the wing with the upward-deflected aileron, further decreasing lift on that side and augmenting the rolling moment.

questions.question: Longerons are described as what kind of structural member?
options: A. Lateral ring members of the fuselage
B. The primary load-carrying lengthwise (longitudinal) members of the aircraft
questions.explanation: Longerons run fore-and-aft along the fuselage (or wing) and are the principal longitudinal load-carrying members in truss and semi-monocoque structures.
